items.en: The tools have expanded too. Following the 2008 financial crisis, when interest rates fell close to zero, many central banks turned to quantitative easing — creating money to buy government bonds and other assets in order to lower long-term borrowing costs. These measures helped stabilise the financial system but also raised difficult questions about inequality, asset prices and the boundaries between monetary and fiscal policy that continue to be debated today.
items.context: C1 reading "Central Banks and the Art of Managing Inflation", paragraph 5

items.en: The Rule of Law and the Independence of Judges
items.context: C2 reading title

items.en: Few political ideals are invoked as frequently, or defined as loosely, as the rule of law. At its most minimal, the phrase denotes a state of affairs in which those who govern are themselves bound by publicly known rules, applied consistently and enforced by courts. It stands in implicit contrast to the rule of men: government by the arbitrary will of whoever happens to hold power.
items.context: C2 reading "The Rule of Law and the Independence of Judges", paragraph 1

items.en: Legal philosophers have long debated how much more the concept should contain. On a 'thin' or formal account, associated with theorists such as Joseph Raz, the rule of law requires that laws be general, prospective, clear, stable and impartially administered — but says nothing about their moral content. A thoroughly unjust regime could, in principle, satisfy these criteria. 'Thick' or substantive accounts, by contrast, insist that the rule of law is inseparable from the protection of fundamental rights, so that a legal order which systematically violates them cannot be said to embody the ideal at all.
items.context: C2 reading "The Rule of Law and the Independence of Judges", paragraph 2

items.en: Whatever one's theoretical commitments, there is broad agreement that judicial independence is indispensable. If judges can be dismissed, intimidated or rewarded by the executive, the promise that power is constrained by law becomes hollow, for those charged with enforcing the constraints would themselves be under the control of those they are meant to constrain. Hence the elaborate safeguards found in many constitutions: security of tenure, protected salaries, and appointment procedures designed to insulate the judiciary from partisan pressure.
items.context: C2 reading "The Rule of Law and the Independence of Judges", paragraph 3

items.en: Independence, however, is not to be confused with unaccountability. Courts derive their authority in large part from the reasoned justification of their decisions, which are published, open to criticism and subject to appeal. A judiciary perceived as pursuing its own political agenda risks forfeiting the very legitimacy on which its independence depends. The balance is delicate, and it is struck differently in different legal traditions.
items.context: C2 reading "The Rule of Law and the Independence of Judges", paragraph 4

items.en: Recent years have furnished numerous examples of governments seeking to reshape courts to their advantage — lowering retirement ages to remove sitting judges, expanding benches to alter majorities, or curtailing judicial review. Such measures are frequently presented as democratic reforms that restore power to elected representatives. Whether they in fact strengthen democracy or hollow it out is precisely the question that the rule of law obliges citizens, and their courts, to ask.
items.context: C2 reading "The Rule of Law and the Independence of Judges", paragraph 5

items.en: Leadership Under Uncertainty
items.context: C2 reading title

items.en: Management textbooks have traditionally portrayed decision-making as a rational sequence: define the problem, gather the relevant information, weigh the options and select the one with the highest expected value. Crises expose the limitations of this model with brutal clarity. When a pandemic spreads, a supply chain collapses or a cyber-attack paralyses an organisation, information is fragmentary, time is scarce and the very nature of the problem may still be unknown.
items.context: C2 reading "Leadership Under Uncertainty", paragraph 1

items.en: Scholars have found it useful to distinguish between risk and uncertainty — a distinction usually traced to the economist Frank Knight. Under risk, the possible outcomes and their probabilities can be estimated, however roughly; under genuine uncertainty, they cannot. Many of the tools leaders rely on, from cost–benefit analysis to financial models, presuppose the former and can foster a dangerous illusion of precision when applied to the latter.
items.context: C2 reading "Leadership Under Uncertainty", paragraph 2

items.en: What, then, distinguishes effective leadership when the map runs out? One recurring finding is the value of acting on provisional judgements while remaining openly willing to revise them. Leaders who wait for certainty often act too late; those who commit irrevocably to an early diagnosis risk compounding their errors. The most capable combine decisiveness with what organisational theorists call 'sensemaking': continually updating their understanding as events unfold, and saying so candidly.
items.context: C2 reading "Leadership Under Uncertainty", paragraph 3

items.en: Communication becomes, in this light, not an adjunct to the response but a central part of it. People can tolerate a remarkable degree of bad news; what corrodes trust is the sense that they are being misled or kept in the dark. Leaders who acknowledge what they do not know, explain the reasoning behind their decisions and set out the conditions under which those decisions might change tend to retain credibility even when particular calls prove mistaken.
items.context: C2 reading "Leadership Under Uncertainty", paragraph 4

items.en: None of this diminishes the importance of preparation. Organisations that have rehearsed scenarios, built redundancy into critical systems and cultivated a culture in which junior staff feel able to raise concerns are better placed to improvise when the unexpected occurs. Paradoxically, it is the discipline of planning that makes flexibility possible: as one military maxim has it, plans are useless, but planning is indispensable.
items.context: C2 reading "Leadership Under Uncertainty", paragraph 5

items.en: Opening a Bank Account
items.context: A1 listening title

items.en: Bank clerk: Good morning. How can I help you? Customer: Good morning. I'd like to open a bank account, please. Bank clerk: Of course. Do you have your passport or ID card with you? Customer: Yes, here's my passport.
items.context: A1 listening script "Opening a Bank Account", part 1

items.en: Bank clerk: Thank you. What's your address? Customer: It's 14 Green Street, flat 3. Bank clerk: And your phone number? Customer: It's 555 21 34 67. Bank clerk: Great. Do you want a debit card too? Customer: Yes, please.
items.context: A1 listening script "Opening a Bank Account", part 2

items.en: Bank clerk: Your card will arrive by post in five days. You can also use our mobile app. It's free. Customer: How much does the account cost? Bank clerk: It's free for students. Are you a student? Customer: Yes, I study at the university.
items.context: A1 listening script "Opening a Bank Account", part 3

items.en: Bank clerk: Perfect. Please sign here and here. Customer: OK. Is that everything? Bank clerk: Yes, that's everything. Welcome to the bank! Customer: Thank you very much. Goodbye.
items.context: A1 listening script "Opening a Bank Account", part 4

items.en: A Phone Call About a Job Advert
items.context: A2 listening title

items.en: Receptionist: Hello, Sunrise Hotel, Maria speaking. How can I help? Giorgi: Hello. I'm calling about the job advert for a part-time receptionist. Is the job still available? Receptionist: Yes, it is. Can I ask your name? Giorgi: Giorgi Beridze.
items.context: A2 listening script "A Phone Call About a Job Advert", part 1

items.en: Receptionist: Thank you, Giorgi. Do you have any experience? Giorgi: Yes, I worked in a café last summer, and I helped at the reception of a guest house for two months. I speak Georgian, English and a little Russian. Receptionist: That's useful. Many of our guests come from abroad.
items.context: A2 listening script "A Phone Call About a Job Advert", part 2

items.en: Giorgi: Could you tell me the working hours? Receptionist: It's three evenings a week, from six to eleven, and one shift at the weekend. Giorgi: That's perfect, because I have lectures in the morning. And what is the pay? Receptionist: It's twelve lari an hour, and you get a free dinner on each shift.
items.context: A2 listening script "A Phone Call About a Job Advert", part 3

items.en: Receptionist: Could you send us your CV by email? The address is jobs@sunrisehotel.example. Giorgi: Of course. I'll send it this afternoon. Receptionist: Great. The manager will call you next week to arrange an interview. Giorgi: Thank you very much for your help. Goodbye.
items.context: A2 listening script "A Phone Call About a Job Advert", part 4

items.en: Team Meeting: Planning a Product Launch
items.context: B1 listening title

items.en: Anna: OK, let's get started. The aim of today's meeting is to agree on a plan for launching our new fitness app in March. We've got about thirty minutes. Luka, could you start with an update on development?
items.context: B1 listening script "Team Meeting: Planning a Product Launch", part 1

items.en: Luka: Sure. The app is about ninety per cent finished. We're still fixing a few problems with the step counter on older phones. To be honest, I think we need two more weeks of testing before we can say it's ready. Anna: Two weeks is fine, as long as we keep the launch date.
items.context: B1 listening script "Team Meeting: Planning a Product Launch", part 2

items.en: Nino: From the marketing side, we'd like to start promoting the app on social media at the end of February. We're planning short videos with a local trainer. The only issue is the budget — the videos will cost more than we expected. Anna: How much more? Nino: About fifteen per cent.
items.context: B1 listening script "Team Meeting: Planning a Product Launch", part 3

items.en: Anna: I'd suggest reducing the number of videos from six to four. That should keep us within budget. Does everyone agree? Luka: That sounds reasonable. Nino: Yes, four good videos are better than six average ones.
items.context: B1 listening script "Team Meeting: Planning a Product Launch", part 4

items.en: Anna: Great. So, to sum up: Luka's team finishes testing by the fifteenth of February, Nino's team prepares four videos, and I'll speak to the finance department about the final budget. Let's meet again next Thursday at the same time. Thanks, everyone.
items.context: B1 listening script "Team Meeting: Planning a Product Launch", part 5

items.en: Job Interview: Tell Me About Yourself
items.context: B1 listening title

items.en: Interviewer: Thanks for coming in, Elene. Let's begin with a classic question: could you tell me a little about yourself? Elene: Of course. I graduated in business administration two years ago, and since then I've been working as a customer service adviser at a telecom company.
items.context: B1 listening script "Job Interview: Tell Me About Yourself", part 1

items.en: Elene: In that role, I handle around forty calls a day, mostly from customers with billing problems. I've learned to stay calm with people who are upset and to explain complicated things in simple words. Last year I was chosen as the team's 'adviser of the month' twice.
items.context: B1 listening script "Job Interview: Tell Me About Yourself", part 2

items.en: Interviewer: That's impressive. Why are you interested in this position as a project coordinator? Elene: I've really enjoyed the parts of my job that involve organising things — for example, I helped plan the training programme for new staff. I'd like to develop those skills further, and your company is known for its well-organised projects.
items.context: B1 listening script "Job Interview: Tell Me About Yourself", part 3

items.en: Interviewer: What would you say is your main weakness? Elene: I used to find it hard to say no when colleagues asked for help, so I sometimes had too much to do. Now I use a simple planning system and I'm honest about deadlines, which has made a big difference.
items.context: B1 listening script "Job Interview: Tell Me About Yourself", part 4

items.en: Interviewer: Do you have any questions for us? Elene: Yes. What does a typical week look like for a coordinator here, and what kind of training do you offer? Interviewer: Good questions. Let me explain…
items.context: B1 listening script "Job Interview: Tell Me About Yourself", part 5

items.en: Radio Phone-In: Is Fast Fashion Worth the Cost?
items.context: B2 listening title

items.en: Presenter: Good afternoon, and welcome to Talkback. Today's question: is fast fashion worth the cost? Cheap clothes are more popular than ever, but critics say the environmental and human price is far too high. Our lines are open. First caller is Sophie. Sophie, go ahead.
items.context: B2 listening script "Radio Phone-In: Is Fast Fashion Worth the Cost?", part 1

items.en: Sophie: Hi. I'm a student, and honestly, I couldn't afford to dress decently without budget shops. I know there are problems, but it's easy for people with good salaries to tell the rest of us to buy expensive, ethical brands. Presenter: That's a fair point. Thanks, Sophie. Next, we have Tom.
items.context: B2 listening script "Radio Phone-In: Is Fast Fashion Worth the Cost?", part 2

items.en: Tom: I work in recycling, and the amount of clothing we receive is staggering. A lot of it has hardly been worn. Most of it can't be recycled into new clothes because the fabrics are mixed, so it ends up in landfill or is shipped abroad. Presenter: So the problem is how much we buy, not just how cheap it is? Tom: Exactly.
items.context: B2 listening script "Radio Phone-In: Is Fast Fashion Worth the Cost?", part 3

items.en: Presenter: Our third caller, Leila, runs a second-hand shop. Leila: I'd say the solution isn't only about money. Second-hand clothes are often cheaper than fast fashion, and repairing things is a skill we've lost. If more people bought fewer, better pieces and looked after them, everyone would benefit.
items.context: B2 listening script "Radio Phone-In: Is Fast Fashion Worth the Cost?", part 4

items.en: Presenter: Some strong views there. It seems our callers agree on one thing: the real issue may be the habit of constant buying. After the news, we'll be speaking to an economist about whether companies or governments should take more responsibility. Stay with us.
items.context: B2 listening script "Radio Phone-In: Is Fast Fashion Worth the Cost?", part 5

items.en: A Negotiation Call with a Supplier
items.context: B2 listening title

items.en: Buyer: Hi, Mark, thanks for making time. I wanted to talk about our order for next quarter. As you know, we're planning to double the volume, so we were hoping for a better unit price. Supplier: Good to hear the business is growing. What did you have in mind?
items.context: B2 listening script "A Negotiation Call with a Supplier", part 1

items.en: Buyer: At the moment we pay four euros per unit. Given the larger volume, we were thinking of three fifty. Supplier: That's quite a big drop. Our raw material costs have gone up this year. The best I could do is three eighty, provided you commit to a twelve-month contract.
items.context: B2 listening script "A Negotiation Call with a Supplier", part 2

items.en: Buyer: Twelve months is a long commitment for us, especially in such an uncertain market. Would you consider three seventy if we signed for nine months instead? And perhaps we could pay within fifteen days rather than thirty, which would help your cash flow.
items.context: B2 listening script "A Negotiation Call with a Supplier", part 3

items.en: Supplier: Faster payment is definitely attractive. All right — three seventy-five for nine months with payment in fifteen days. But we'd need the first order confirmed by the end of the month so we can plan production. Buyer: I think we can work with that. Could you also include free delivery for orders over five thousand units?
items.context: B2 listening script "A Negotiation Call with a Supplier", part 4

items.en: Supplier: I'll have to check with our logistics team, but I don't see why not. I'll send you a written proposal by Friday. Buyer: Perfect. Once I've reviewed it with our finance director, we can finalise everything next week.
items.context: B2 listening script "A Negotiation Call with a Supplier", part 5

items.en: Lecture: How Central Banks Fight Inflation
items.context: C1 listening title

items.en: Good morning. Today I want to look at a question that has dominated economic news in recent years: how do central banks try to bring inflation under control, and why does it so often feel as though they are steering a ship with a very delayed rudder?
items.context: C1 listening script "Lecture: How Central Banks Fight Inflation", part 1

items.en: Let's start with the basic mechanism. When a central bank raises its policy rate, commercial banks typically raise the rates they charge on loans and mortgages. Borrowing becomes more expensive, saving becomes more attractive, and overall demand in the economy tends to slow. In theory, weaker demand reduces the pressure on prices.
items.context: C1 listening script "Lecture: How Central Banks Fight Inflation", part 2

items.en: The catch is timing. Most estimates suggest that the full effect of a rate change on inflation takes somewhere between twelve and twenty-four months. So policymakers are effectively making decisions today based on where they think the economy will be in a year or two — and forecasts, as you will discover in your careers, are frequently wrong.
items.context: C1 listening script "Lecture: How Central Banks Fight Inflation", part 3

items.en: This is why expectations matter so much. If households and firms believe inflation will stay high, they behave in ways that make it stay high: workers demand larger pay rises, and businesses raise prices in advance. A credible central bank can break this cycle simply by convincing people that it will do whatever is necessary. Communication, in other words, is a policy tool in its own right.
items.context: C1 listening script "Lecture: How Central Banks Fight Inflation", part 4

items.en: Finally, there is the question of cost. Raising rates too far or too fast risks a recession and rising unemployment, and those costs are not shared equally. For next week, I'd like you to read the article on the reading list comparing two recent tightening cycles, and come prepared to discuss whether the central banks involved acted too early, too late, or about right.
items.context: C1 listening script "Lecture: How Central Banks Fight Inflation", part 5

items.en: Podcast: The Psychology of Good Decisions
items.context: C1 listening title

items.en: Host: Welcome back to Mind Matters. My guest today has spent twenty years studying how professionals make decisions under pressure — doctors, pilots and investors among them. Dr Okafor, thanks for joining us. Guest: My pleasure.
items.context: C1 listening script "Podcast: The Psychology of Good Decisions", part 1

items.en: Host: Let's start with the obvious question. Why do intelligent, experienced people make bad decisions? Guest: Mostly not because they lack knowledge, but because of predictable patterns in how we think. One is overconfidence. Experts in particular tend to overestimate how accurate their judgements are, especially in fields where feedback is slow or unclear.
items.context: C1 listening script "Podcast: The Psychology of Good Decisions", part 2

items.en: Host: Can that be fixed? Guest: To some extent. One technique I recommend is the 'pre-mortem'. Before committing to a decision, a team imagines that it is a year later and the project has failed. Each person then writes down why it failed. It sounds pessimistic, but it gives people permission to voice doubts that they might otherwise keep to themselves.
items.context: C1 listening script "Podcast: The Psychology of Good Decisions", part 3

items.en: Host: What about gut feeling? Some people swear by it. Guest: Intuition is valuable when it's been trained in an environment with regular, quick feedback — a chess player or an experienced firefighter, say. It's far less reliable in areas like long-term investing, where outcomes are noisy and arrive years later. The key is knowing which kind of environment you're in.
items.context: C1 listening script "Podcast: The Psychology of Good Decisions", part 4

items.en: Host: Last question: one habit our listeners could adopt tomorrow? Guest: Keep a decision journal. Write down important decisions, what you expected to happen and why. Months later, compare. It's humbling, but it's one of the few ways to get honest feedback on your own judgement.
items.context: C1 listening script "Podcast: The Psychology of Good Decisions", part 5

items.en: Panel: Who Should Regulate Artificial Intelligence?
items.context: C2 listening title

items.en: Moderator: Good evening. Tonight's panel addresses a deceptively simple question: who should regulate artificial intelligence, and how? With me are a technology lawyer, a computer scientist and a former trade negotiator. Let me start with you, Ms Varga. Is existing law adequate?
items.context: C2 listening script "Panel: Who Should Regulate Artificial Intelligence?", part 1

items.en: Lawyer: In part. A great deal of harm caused by AI systems — discrimination in hiring, defective products, privacy breaches — is already unlawful. The difficulty lies less in the absence of rules than in their enforcement. When a decision emerges from a model that even its developers struggle to explain, establishing causation and liability becomes extraordinarily hard.
items.context: C2 listening script "Panel: Who Should Regulate Artificial Intelligence?", part 2

items.en: Scientist: I'd add that the technology is moving faster than any legislative process can. Rules written around today's architectures may well be obsolete within a few years. That argues for regulating outcomes and risks rather than specific techniques — requiring, say, rigorous testing and independent audits for high-stakes uses, whatever the underlying method.
items.context: C2 listening script "Panel: Who Should Regulate Artificial Intelligence?", part 3

items.en: Negotiator: And let's not pretend this can be settled nationally. The leading developers operate across borders, and capital and talent flow to wherever the regime is most permissive. Without a degree of international coordination — on safety standards at the very least — unilateral rules risk being either circumvented or simply ignored.
items.context: C2 listening script "Panel: Who Should Regulate Artificial Intelligence?", part 4

items.en: Moderator: So, to summarise the emerging consensus: existing law covers more than is often assumed, but enforcement, adaptability and international coordination are the weak points. Ms Varga, a final word? Lawyer: Only that regulation is not the enemy of innovation. Clear rules, sensibly drafted, give responsible developers the certainty they need to invest.
items.context: C2 listening script "Panel: Who Should Regulate Artificial Intelligence?", part 5

items.en: Crisis Briefing: Responding to a Data Breach
items.context: C2 listening title

items.en: Chief Executive: Thank you all for joining at such short notice. I'll be brief and as candid as I can. At around two o'clock this morning, our security team detected unauthorised access to one of our customer databases. The intrusion has been contained, but we must assume that some customer data has been exposed.
items.context: C2 listening script "Crisis Briefing: Responding to a Data Breach", part 1

items.en: Chief Executive: Here is what we know. The affected system held names, email addresses and order histories for approximately two hundred thousand customers. Here is what we do not yet know: whether payment details were accessed. Our current evidence suggests not, since card data is stored separately and encrypted, but I am not prepared to say so definitively until the forensic investigation is complete.
items.context: C2 listening script "Crisis Briefing: Responding to a Data Breach", part 2

items.en: Head of Legal: We have notified the data protection authority, as we are required to do, and we will be writing to every affected customer today. The message will set out plainly what happened, what information was involved and what steps they should take — in particular, to be alert to phishing emails that may appear to come from us.
items.context: C2 listening script "Crisis Briefing: Responding to a Data Breach", part 3

items.en: Head of Communications: Externally, our position is straightforward: we will not speculate, we will not minimise, and we will update customers and the press at fixed times — nine a.m. and five p.m. daily — until the investigation concludes. Internally, please direct every media enquiry to my team; consistency matters more than speed.
items.context: C2 listening script "Crisis Briefing: Responding to a Data Breach", part 4

items.en: Chief Executive: Let me be clear about one last thing. The question of how this happened will be answered fully and independently, and lessons will be acted upon. But our priority for the next forty-eight hours is the people whose trust we have put at risk. Questions?
items.context: C2 listening script "Crisis Briefing: Responding to a Data Breach", part 5
